title: Name and life cycle of a single attempt: 'dispatch'
body: Earlier decisions already speak of 'first dispatch' and 'the current dispatch'. Proposal: a Dispatch is one identified delivery of work (an assignment, handoff or message) to one agent session generation. Its states are: created → nudged → delivered (the agent fetched it) → working → stopped, where stopped means a result, a blocked report or a decision request, or → unknown. A retry, a correction after rejection, or a resumption after a crash is always a new dispatch, and only evidence correlated to the current dispatch counts. The assignment has its own states: active → result submitted → accepted, or rejected (back to active, same worker), or needs reconciliation, or cancelled. Alternative: call it an 'attempt' instead.
rec: Adopt 'Dispatch' as defined, keeping the assignment and dispatch life cycles separate. It reuses the language from the adapter and runtime decisions, so there's no new synonym.

title: How are side effects recorded so recovery can tell what already happened?
body: After a crash, the owning leader has to work out what a worker actually did. Options: (A) Record effects as they happen. Workers record each consequential effect, such as commit, push, PR create or update, comment, or file outside the workspace, with `asmai effect` immediately after doing it, tagged with the dispatch. The final result also lists them. (B) Effects are listed only in the final result. (C) Effects aren't recorded, and the leader inspects git and GitHub after the fact.
rec: A. A running effect ledger gives reconciliation a trail even when the final result never arrives. It is evidence, not proof: the leader still checks the real repository or GitHub state before acting, because an effect can happen without being recorded.
options: B: only in the final result
C: no record; inspect after the fact

title: Who decides how to recover an assignment that needs reconciliation?
body: Options: (A) The owning leader inspects the effect ledger, real repository and PR state, and the transcript where available. It records what is known, what is unknown and its choice: continue with a new dispatch to the same worker, use a fresh worker, abandon, or escalate. The existing authority rule applies, so Phillip is asked only when distinct viable recovery approaches remain or when the needed action is outside the mandate. (B) Phillip is always asked after a crash or unknown state.
rec: A. Recovery is ordinary leader work under the existing mandate and the 'distinct viable approaches' rule, and the reconciliation record is a delegated decision record. Coordination tells you when reconciliation changed the plan or found effects that cannot be undone.
options: A: owning leader decides under existing authority rules

title: What happens to a dispatch that goes silent?
body: Hooks can be lost, and an agent can hang. Options: (A) If a working dispatch shows no correlated lifecycle observation for a configured period, it becomes 'unknown'. The daemon tells the owning leader and does not kill or retry anything on its own. The leader checks the agent, for example through status or by asking a human to attach, and then reconciles. (B) After the period, the daemon interrupts the agent and lets the retry rules apply.
rec: A. Silence never implies failure or success, and it triggers a check, not an action. Duplicate, late or out-of-order observations go into the journal, but only current-dispatch observations change state, and conflicting ones also lead to 'unknown'. The timeout values belong to the operating limits ticket.
options: A: mark unknown, notify leader, no auto action

title: How does a leader regain its per-job context after a restart?
body: The roles decision says one leader per role serves all jobs, with separate context for each job. Options: (A) The store is the source of truth. On every start, and whenever it switches job, a leader gets a store-generated brief per job (`asmai brief <job>`) covering open handoffs, assignments, pending decisions, grants and recent journal entries. Native session resume is only a convenience. (B) Rely on the provider's native session resume and use the store only as a fallback.
rec: A. Provider conversations aren't guaranteed to survive or move between hosts, and one long session for all jobs would bloat. Briefs keep per-job context separate and make leader restarts routine, while native resume adds conversational memory when it works.
options: A: store briefs are canonical; native resume optional
